name: Cree, Plains
sweep_summary: Plains Cree is in the catalog as 'excluded' (reason sources-undetermined: secondary-stress direction fork between Wolfart 1996:431 'either direction' and Okimasis & Ratt 1999 leftward; our check of 9/16 already holds Athanasopoulou et al. 2025 JIPA, Muehlbauer 2006, Cook 1991 and Wolfart 1973). Two works with stress in the title. (1) Wolfart 1989 'Prosodische Grenzsignale im Plains Cree' (Folia Linguistica 23:327-334) is closed (Unpaywall/Crossref/De Gruyter bot wall/HathiTrust search-only/no repository copy); I read three of its six citing works (Russell 1998 ZASPiL, Russell 2006/2008 sandhi draft, Shwayder 2015 diss., all downloaded to plus the held Wolvengrey 2011: all cite it only for word-boundary vowel sandhi/devoicing (kâ+i -> kê in realis clauses, sandhi in casual speech), none for stress placement, so relevance is unclear (boundary prosody, possibly including antepenult stress as a boundary signal); priority medium because a first-hand Wolfart statement from 1989 could bear on the 1996 direction fork. (2) Cook 1991 (Glottolog wrongly credits editor Cowan) was held by the project and re-read: antepenultimate primary accent, postlexical, with penult alternants from post-stress vowel/glide deletion; silent on secondary stress, so it refines but cannot close the fork; it is the best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title and does not supersede the catalog's deciding sources. Two side findings for the parent: (a) the archive.org 'rosettaproject_crk_detail-1' item marked OPEN ONLINE for Wolfart 1996 in is a one-page excerpt (p. 390, Introduction) and does not contain p. 431 (saved, checked); (b) the held Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 OSF draft (litreview/sources) reproduces Wolfart 1996:431's examples with feet marked ('adapted to the IPA and feet have been indicated', fn. 8): nêhiyaw /(ˈneː)(hiˌjaw)/ and pasakwâpisimowin /(ˌpa)(saˌkwaː)(piˈsi)(moˌwin)/, i.e. they read Wolfart's secondaries as bidirectional with a final secondary in trisyllables, which is exactly the reading the exclusion note calls unresolvable from scanned; second-hand, but worth logging against the fork. written in the save directory;org/HathiTrust/Penn DSpace/ZASPiL/UManitoba APIs and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: The word stress or accent in Cree is largely predicted by a postlexical antepenultimate stress rule where rules of lexical derivation are organized in two or three strata. [...] Needless to say, there is a lot more to be learned of Cree stress or accent, but the analysis presented in this paper demonstrates the regularity of an antipenultimate stress where apparent counterexamples are accounted for in level ordered lexical derivation. Another point to be emphasized here is that "stress" is clearly an inadequate term as indicated by the stability phenomenon. I suggest that "accent" is a more appropriate term to use until more is known about the rhythmic pattern of Cree.
new_statements.citation: Cook, Eung-Do. 1991. Lexical derivation and stress in Cree. In William Cowan (ed.), Papers of the Twenty-Second Algonquian Conference, 21-29. Ottawa: Carleton University.
new_statements.reading: Fixed antepenultimate primary stress (better: accent) in polysyllabic nouns and verbs, assigned postlexically before optional vowel/glide deletions that create surface penult alternants; no statement on secondary stress, its direction, or disyllables; based on two speakers' citation forms.

Another point to be emphasized here is…

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Cook 1991 (PAC 22: 21-29) is a first-hand (two northern-Alberta Plains Cree speakers, citation forms) statement of PRIMARY stress only: antepenultimate in polysyllabic nouns and verbs, assigned postlexically, with surface penult/antepenult alternants explained by later i-deletion, glide deletion and stress relinking (rules (8) p. 24, (14) p. 27). It marks "only the strongest stress of a word" (p. 21), makes no statement on secondary stress or its direction, and leaves the one underived disyllable in its paradigm (3sg nipaaw, (2a) p. 22) unmarked; the derived disyllables in (7) p. 24 (ntápin,…

audit.recode_to: Keep classification excluded. Rewrite the exclusion reason from 'stress not determinable from the sources' to: 'word-stress status rejected/contested by instrumental work — Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 (IJAL 91:97-147): no word stress, phrase language (H.. LHLH phrasal tones); Athanasopoulou, Goddard & Flynn 2025 (JIPA 55:92-133, pp. 92, 128-129): predictable penult HL word-level pitch accent, not stress, duration not a cue; Muehlbauer 2006 (PAC 37:229-268): penult pitch fall; all three reject the antepenult-primary + alternating-secondary profile StressTyp2 codes from Wolfart 1996:431 / Okimasis & Ratt 1999:3-4, whose own statements disagree on secondary direction and which Wolfart 1973 fn. 58 called highly tentative.' Add these to refs/sources with the page locators above; the StressTyp2 contradiction note stands and is strengthened.
audit.deciding_source_year: 1996 (Wolfart HNAI sketch) vs 1999/2018 (Okimasis & Ratt pedagogical grammar) vs 1973 (Wolfart grammar); backed since 2026-08-18 by Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 (instrumental)
audit.reasoning: Record: classification excluded, no quote, reason 'not determinable from the sources' after the 18 Aug 2026 rejudge (Wolfart 1996:431 'either direction' vs Okimasis & Ratt 1999:3-4 leftward-only; Wolfart 1973 states no rule). I confirmed the Okimasis passage verbatim in the held 2018 open edition (pp. 6-7), the Wolfart 1973 hedges verbatim in the archive.org text downloaded now, and the Schmirler & Arnhold 2025 conclusion in the held OSF draft; the HNAI 17:431 page itself is not yet obtained (no open copy) but is corroborated via StressTyp2's passage bank and an independent page-cited quotation. Web search turned up a second 2025 instrumental study we did not have — Athanasopoulou, Goddard & Flynn, JIPA 55 (open access, downloaded, read pp. 92, 128-130): it too rejects antepenult stress and alternating rhythm, but unlike Schmirler & Arnhold it posits a predictable word-level penult HL pitch accent and says the languag

sources.note: The only dedicated pre-2006 paper on Plains Cree stress placement (antepenult 'accent' rule with paradigm-internal penult alternants); documents that even the antepenult camp hedged ('not so transparent as to be fully predictable').

sources.citation: Wolfart, H. Christoph. 1973. Plains Cree: A Grammatical Study. Transactions of the American Philosophical Society n.s. 63(5). Philadelphia. (archive.org scanned text)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: fn. 58: 'these observations must be considered highly tentative since the data are not without contradictions. A detailed study of Cree stress and pitch phenomena is required before a fuller statement can be attempted.' Appendix A 0.1: 'the status of the semivowels, syllable structure, the phonological delimitation of the word, and the stress, pitch, and intonation system seem most urgently in need of investigation... For a brief discussion of stress... see Bloomfield, 1930: pp. 1-6.' No stress-placement rule is stated anywhere in the grammar.

sources.quote: p. 92: 'We find that there are cues supporting both previous claims: a high F0 on the antepenultimate syllable compatible with "antepenultimate stress" and a falling F0 on the penultimate syllable compatible with "penultimate accent." Tonal patterns in other syllables are the result of prosodic boundaries, phonetic interpolation, or tonal spreading.' p. 128: 'If we discount the possibilities of Plains Cree being a stress or tone language, we are left
sources.locator: abstract p. 92; s.5.4 p. 128; s.6 Conclusions p. 129
sources.note: Second, independent 2025 acoustic study not previously in our record; rejects antepenult stress but argues for a word-level penult HL pitch accent — must be cited alongside Schmirler & Arnhold so the exclusion reason reads 'word-stress status contested/rejected instrumentally', not flatly 'no word stress'.

sources.citation: Muehlbauer, Jeff. 2006. Pitch as accent in Plains Cree nominals. In H.C. Wolfart (ed.), Actes du 37e Congres des Algonquinistes, 229-268. Winnipeg: University of Manitoba.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Conclusion: 'the penultimate syllable of a "word" will consistently have a low or dropping pitch... Plains Cree uses a falling fundamental frequency to express phonological prominences. In the typology of prominence systems, this means that Plains Cree is not a prototypical case of any of the categories used by linguists ("stress," "pitch accent," or "tone").' p. 260: 'the pitch prominence is usually two syllables from an edge, which implicates a bisyllabic, trochaic foot'. Acoustic (F0) study of spontaneous speech; no alternating secondary stresses reported.
sources.locator: pp. 229-230 (three prior accounts: Bloomfield 1930 antepenult, Edwards 1954 penult, Lacombe 1874 ultima); pp. 259-260; Conclusion p. 261
sources.note: The first acoustic account (penult pitch fall, trochaic foot at right edge); the 'penult' arm of the three-way split both 2025 studies build on.

sources.citation: Cook, Eung-Do. 1991. Lexical derivation and stress in Cree. In William Cowan (ed.), Papers of the Twenty-Second Algonquian Conference, 21-29. Ottawa: Carleton University. [Glottolog 674475 lists the editor Cowan as author; the paper is by Cook]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 21: 'Stress has never been considered phonemic in Cree, but it is not so transparent as to be fully predictable at the phonetic surface. According to H.C. Wolfart (personal communication), the general assumption of antepenultimate stress, as exemplified by the noun and verb paradigms given in (1) and (2), is unable to account for all stress patterns in Cree.' p. 22: 'Stress falls regularly on the antepenultimate syllable regardless of whether the word is uninflected or inflected'. p. 28: 'The word stress or accent in Cree is largely predicted by a postlexical antepenultimate stress rule'.
sources.note: Data from two Plains Cree speakers (northern Alberta), citation forms, only the strongest stress marked. Primary stress/accent falls on the antepenultimate syllable in nouns and verbs regardless of inflection; apparent penult stress in some paradigm forms (e.g. 'shoe' paradigm, p. 23) results from optional elision of an underlyingly stressed antepenult vowel or a glide (i-deletion, glide deletion) after stress assignment, with rightward 'stress relinking'; the antepenultimate rule is postlexical, preceded by level-ordered lexical rules (stem-vowel deletion, C-copy, y-epenthesis). Says nothing…

sources.citation: Lacombe, Albert (1874). Grammaire de la langue des Cris. Montréal: C.O. Beauchemin & Valois. iii+190 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Lacombe's 'accent' means vowel length (long vs short a, i), not stress; the grammar has no word-stress or prominence statement, so it neither supports nor contradicts the catalog's antepenultimate reading (Cook 1991). Whole 199-page text layer a full-text search for stress/accent/accentu/prosod/tonique/syllabe/prononc/voix/ton; the only other hits are 'ton' = 'your', 'ton de voix' in verb glosses (kisimow 'he has an angry tone of voice'), reduplicative diminutive (p. 13), and initial change ('changement', p. 155). Note PuRe tags the item ISO 639-3 csw (Swampy Cree), but Lacombe's preface says…
